### Preparation
#### Downloading raw data to hummingbird
First, you must sftp your raw MinIon files into hummingbird. Make a directory (`mkdir`) with the name of your MinIon Run and 3-letter species name. For example, my MinIon run was #42 and my species name is AAR, so I sftp my raw files into the following location(`pwd`): `/hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/42_AAR`
  
  
#### Making `files` directory for guppy basecaller slurm
Next, make another directory at the same level as the previous called "files". This is where we'll store the guppy basecaller slurm file.For example, my location looks like this:
`/hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/files`  
  
    
#### Making `fastq` directory for guppy basecaller output
Finally, make another directory for the guppy basecaller output. At the same level as the previous two directories, you're going to make a directory with the name of your MinIon Run. Within this directory, make another called `fastq`. For example, my location looks like this:
`/hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/RUN_42/fastq`


### Guppy Basecaller
Inside of the `files` directory, create(`nano`) the following slurm.

``` {bash eval = FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=guppy
#SBATCH --output=guppy_RUN_42.out
#SBATCH --error=guppy_RUN_42.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=ALL
#SBATCH --mail-user=asawkins@ucsc.edu #your email here
#SBATCH --partition=128x24
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --exclusive
#SBATCH --ntasks-per-node=24

# Above are all the specifics SLURM needs to run your specific job.

# --ntasks-per-node will be used in doParallel.R to specify the number
# of cores to use on the machine. Using 24

# now load programs needed

module load guppy


#run the command:


guppy_basecaller -c dna_r10.4_e8.1_sup.cfg --num_callers 24 --device cuda:0 --input_path /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/42_AAR/ --save_path /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/RUN_42/fastq
```

#### Notes:

* Be sure that your input_path matches the location of your raw files and the save_path matches the empty `fastq` directory you just created.
* You can check the status of the guppy slurm by `nano`ing your output file.




### Concatenate all files into the BigFile  
Inside of the guppy basecaller output directory will be a directory called `pass`. For example, my location looks like this: `/hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/RUN_42/fastq/pass`. These are sequences that have 'passed'.  
Inside of this directory run the following, but change AAR = your species name and 42 = your MinIon run.  
`cat * > AAR_42_BigFile.fastq` 
  
  
Make a directory called `BigFiles` inside of your `files` directory. The location should look like this:
`/hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/files/BigFiles`  
  
  
Move the your concatenated file into the BigFiles directory with this code: `mv AAR_42_BigFile.fastq /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/files/BigFiles`  
  
  
If you have several runs, combine them into one BigFile. `cat AAR_42_BigFile_new.fastq AAR_43_BigFile_new.fastq > AAR_42_43_BigFile.fastq`

### Quality Checks: fastq_info and fastQC
We'll check for fastq errors. First make sure your concatenated fastq files have correctly merged using Fastq Utils (v0.25.1).
``` {bash eval = FALSE}
#load miniconda
module load miniconda3.9

#activate fastq_utils
conda activate /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/programs/fastq_utils_v0.25.1

#run command
fastq_info AAR_42_43_BigFile.fastq.gz
```

It'll spit out the following output.

``` {bash eval = FALSE}
fastq_utils 0.25.1
DEFAULT_HASHSIZE=39000001
Scanning and indexing all reads from AAR_42_43_BigFile.fastq.gz
Read name provided with no suffix
1500000Scanning complete.

Reads processed: 1598015
Memory used in indexing: ~401 MB
------------------------------------
Number of reads: 1598015
Quality encoding range: 34 123
Quality encoding: sanger
Read length: 30 685969 5805
OK
```


Then run FastQC (v0.11.7) on bigfile to get more detailed QC info on the reads:

``` {bash eval = FALSE}
module load fastqc

module load java    #may not be necessary anymore, but if you get a java error, try loading this module


fastqc  AAR_42_43_BigFile.fastq.gz -t 24 -o /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/allyson/MinIon/files/BigFiles/fastqc
```





### Porechop: Removes primers from reads
First gzip your BigFile, `gzip AAR_42_43_BigFile.fastq` then you are ready to go.
```{bash eval = FALSE}
conda activate /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/programs/porechop_v2.4

porechop -i AAR_42_43_BigFile.fastq.gz -o AAR_42_43_BigFile_pc.fastq --threads 24
```
  
  
The input (-i) is your gzip BigFile and the output (-o) is the same name but with "pc" for Porechop and no gz (it is not gzip).

## Nanofilt
We're going to create two filtered sets of reads from the “bigfile”: one for longer reads of lower quality and one for shorter reads of higher quality.  
In either case, 1000 or 500bp is the minimum size. Q value is quality.

Create two slurms, still in the BigFile directory.

name: nanofilt_AAR_42_43_1000q3.slurm

```{bash eval = FALSE}

#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=nanofilt
#SBATCH --output=nanofilt_AAR_42_43_1000q3.out
#SBATCH --error=nanofilt_AAR_42_43_1000q3.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=ALL
#SBATCH --mail-user=asawkins@ucsc.edu
#SBATCH --partition=128x24
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --mem=120
#SBATCH --ntasks=24

# Above are all the specifics SLURM needs to run your specific job.

# --ntasks-per-node will be used in doParallel.R to specify the number
# of cores to use on the machine. Using 24
# now load programs needed

#run the command:

module load miniconda3.9

conda activate /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/programs/nanofilt

gunzip -c AAR_42_43_BigFile_pc.fastq.gz | NanoFilt -q 3 -l 1000 | gzip > AAR_42_43_BigFile_pc_1000q3.fastq.gz
```


name: nanofilt_AAR_42_43_500q5.slurm

```{bash eval = FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=nanofilt

# --ntasks-per-node will be used in doParallel.R to specify the number
# of cores to use on the machine. Using 24
# now load programs needed

#run the command:

module load miniconda3.9

conda activate /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/programs/nanofilt

gunzip -c AAR_42_43_BigFile_pc.fastq.gz | NanoFilt -q 5 -l 500 | gzip > AAR_42_43_BigFile_pc_500q5.fastq.gz
```



##### next align long reads into scaffolds using two different approaches: once using only the reads > 1000bp, and once using all reads > 500 bp



name: wtdbg2_AAR_42_43_1000q3.slurm

```{bash eval = FALSE}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --job-name=wtdbg2
#SBATCH --output=wtdbg2_AAR_42_43_1000q3.out
#SBATCH --error=wtdbg2_AAR_42_43_1000q3.err
#SBATCH --mail-type=ALL
#SBATCH --mail-user=asawkins@ucsc.edu
#SBATCH --partition=128x24
#SBATCH --nodes=1
#SBATCH --mem=120
#SBATCH --ntasks=24


#run the command:

module load miniconda3.9

conda activate /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/programs/wtdbg2


wtdbg2 -x ont -g 600m -t 24 -L 1000 -i AAR_42_43_BigFile_pc_1000q3.fastq.gz -fo AAR_42_43_BigFile_ont_1000q3 #reads > 1000bp
```

## Minimap2: maps your clean_raw reads to your assembly with minimap

```{bash eval = FALSE}
module load miniconda3.9

conda activate /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/programs/minimap2

minimap2 -ax map-ont -t 24 AAR_42_43_BigFile_ont_1000q3.ctg.fa AAR_42_43_BigFile_pc_500q5.fastq.gz > AAR_42_43_1000_500_q3q5_mmap.sam
```



## Racon: makes a consensus sequence

```{bash eval = FALSE}
conda activate /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/programs/racon

racon -u -m 5 -x -4 -g -8 -w 500 -t 24 AAR_42_43_BigFile_pc_500q5.fastq.gz AAR_42_43_1000_500_q3q5_mmap.sam AAR_42_43_BigFile_ont_1000q3.ctg.fa > AAR_42_43_1000_500_q3q5_racon.fasta
```


## final assembly stats
```{bash eval = FALSE}
module load miniconda3.9

conda activate /hb/groups/bernardi_lab/programs/assembly_stats

assembly-stats AAR_42_43_1000_500_q3q5_racon.fasta > AAR_42_43_1000_500_q3q5_racon.fasta_assemblystats
```
